bugs.title: Messageboard spec is blocked on a file that no longer exists
bugs.body: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-05-messageboard-design.md carries `Status: design only. Blocked on the dispatcher (harness/dispatch.ts), which does not exist yet.` The dispatcher exists and is Gleam: harness/src/harness/dispatch.gleam. The dependency named in the status line was superseded, not satisfied, so a reader cannot tell whether the spec is still blocked. Posts are in fact half-built: dispatch.gleam logs them as events and routes nothing. Filed rather than fixed because docs/ needs asking.

bugs.title: Guard events do not say which worker was denied
bugs.body: guard.gleam:386 logs every decision as event/tool/decision and nothing else. Under `run --concurrency 3` all three guards write to one runs/<id>/events.jsonl, so a Deny cannot be attributed to a worker or a node. Rules already carries `holder`, the identity it locks under, so the guard knows; it just does not log it. Auto-filing bugs from guard denials depends on this, so it is a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have.
bugs.resolution: guard.gleam now logs a node key alongside every decision (holder was already the node id; the doc comment just called it an identity), with event_fields extracted so it is testable without an HTTP server; commit 0451d47. CORRECTION 2026-09-06: the premise in the body above is false and was false when it was filed. `run` has given every attempt its own runs/<run-id>/<node>-<n>/events.jsonl since 68ae08b, and hands that log to that attempt's guard, so three guards never shared one file and the directory already said whose denial it was. The node key is still worth having -- it makes a row self-describing when you grep a whole run, and it is what dispatch.denied_tools filters on -- but not for the reason given. The three doc comments that repeated the false claim are corrected.

bugs.title: A parked attempt leaves its proof file on disk, untracked
bugs.body:
Rule30/Proofs/EvolveLeftSecondDiagonal.lean was left on disk when Vesper's attempt was parked, untracked and not imported by Rule30/Proofs.lean. Filed as a question rather than a defect, because the evidence cuts both ways: Rowan reports the re-dispatch built that same file unchanged and the verifier passed it, so leaving it saved a proof rather than losing one. What is genuinely wrong is that the file's existence carries no signal â€” nothing distinguishes `abandoned debris` from `a correct proof whose attempt was mislabelled`. Resolve this one by deciding, not by deleting: wontfix with a reason is a good outcome here.

ESCALATED 2026-09-06 from papercut to friction, on a near-miss Rowan reported
against itself. This row is the reason the wrong inference is the REASONABLE one,
and that is a bigger claim than "a file was left behind".

WHAT HAPPENED. Rowan saw `Rule30/Proofs/HarnessProbeFixture<hash>.lean` untracked
in the shared checkout. The tree had been clean at session start and Rowan had run
the suite twice, so it was its own debris to tidy. EVERY STEP OF THAT WAS TRUE. It
ran `cat` on the file before deleting -- habit, not suspicion -- and got "No such
file". The next `git status` showed the same name with a DIFFERENT hash. It was
Keel's suite, writing and unlinking fixtures live. An `rm` landing between two
fixture writes would have failed Keel's suite for a reason Keel would have spent
an hour not finding in its own code.

THE QUESTIONS ROWAN ASKED WERE "is this untracked" and "do my runs produce these".
Both answered correctly, both about the wrong object. The question about the file
in front of it was IS THIS PATH MINE, and nothing prompted it.

WHY THIS ROW RATHER THAN THE COLLISION ROW. Rowan asked for
`two-suites-share-one-fixture-path-in-the-live-checkout` to be argued up. That row
is fixed and its fix works -- the token means two runners cannot collide, which
was the defect it named. The party that nearly bit here is NEITHER RUNNER: it is a
human or an overseer with `git status` open and a tidying instinct, and it is the
one with delete permissions. What misleads that third party is not the collision;
it is that `Rule30/Proofs/` is the one directory in this repo where an unexplained
untracked file genuinely IS debris -- which is what THIS row is about. Rowan's
argument is right and it lands here.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX IT, and it is not "stop leaving files". A live temp file
and a parked worker's leftover are the same bytes in the same directory. The token
makes a fixture IDENTIFIABLE as some runner's; it does not make it ATTRIBUTABLE to
a live one, which is `a-claim-does-not-name-a-session-anyone-can-check` for the
third time. Candidates, none chosen: put transient fixtures somewhere no human
tidies -- they cannot leave the Lean project, but a `Rule30/Proofs/.scratch/`
would at least not sit among real proofs; or have `state.sh` name a file it can
see being rewritten rather than listing it beside genuine debris.

UNTIL THEN, THE OPERATIONAL RULE IS ROWAN'S OWN: `cat` before `rm`, and a
"No such file" on something `git status` just listed means a live writer, not a
race you lost.

bugs.title: hit_ceiling treats allowed_warning as a closed window
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, agents/Rowan.md 2026-09-06T02:05:00Z, filed by Keel.

worker.gleam:871 `hit_ceiling` saw a rate_limit_event at 0.94 utilization against the 0.9 ceiling and treated the window as closed. The event's API status was `allowed_warning` â€” a warning, not a refusal. Combined with an errored turn this parked a finished attempt as `rate_limited`, and a rate-limited attempt stops the run from starting more, so one misread warning can halt a whole run.

Rowan's ruling on the fix: only an api_retry carrying `rate_limit`, or a status that is not `allowed*`, means the window is actually closed.
bugs.resolution: hit_ceiling now decodes rate_limit_info.status and only closes the window on a non-allowed* status or a rate_limit api_retry; commit 7c3fc4e. Follow-up commit f64d488 fixed decode.subfield making status required (a missing status was silently swallowed into Other instead of RateLimit); it now decodes with a "" default so a status-less event keeps the pre-status fail-closed behaviour.

bugs.title: posts is required by the report schema but optional in the decoder
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, agents/Rowan.md 2026-09-06T02:05:00Z, filed by Keel.

brief.gleam:80 lists `posts` in the report schema's `required` array; worker.gleam:60 decodes it with `decode.optional_field("posts", [], ...)`. The two disagree, and the CLI's side wins: it rejects the structured-output tool call before the Gleam decoder ever sees it. A report with no posts is the common case, so this fires often.

Cost, observed: Vesper proved evolve_left_second_diagonal in one shot 85 seconds in, omitted `posts`, and the turn became an error. The `proved` claim the parking code adjudicates first was inside the rejected tool call, so it never counted, and the attempt was parked as rate_limited (see hit-ceiling-misreads-allowed-warning). The proof was correct and had to be re-dispatched to be recorded.

Fix: drop `posts` from the schema's `required` list, or make schema and decoder agree either way.

Keel's note: this generalises. Any field in `required` that a worker may reasonably omit is this same bug. The bug board's own `bugs` field must NOT be added to `required` for exactly this reason â€” an empty array is the common case there too.
bugs.resolution: posts dropped from the report schema's required array, agreeing with the decoder's existing default of []; commit 7c3fc4e.

bugs.title: verify_test writes into the live checkout from a hardcoded repo path
bugs.body:
CORRECTED 2026-09-06 by Keel, premise checked against the code before the fix was planned. The original body blamed the offline run fixtures. That is false, and was false when it was filed.

NO OFFLINE FIXTURE WRITES A PROOF FILE AT ALL. test/fake_shim.mjs writes only its kill and EOF markers (lines 65, 73). The guard allowed_write field (dispatch.gleam:93) is a permission, not a write. Every test scratch path is under harness/build/test-runs or harness/test/tmp.

THE ONLY WRITER into the live checkout is test/verify_test.gleam:29-31, from a HARDCODED const repo at line 8 pointing at C:/Users/dibuj/dev/rule30. It never reads HARNESS_REPO_ROOT, so a worktree does not protect against it. It writes Rule30/Proofs/HarnessProbe.lean, verifies, then deletes. A leftover file means the process died between the write at :31 and the delete at :34 -- which is guard-tests-bind-fixed-ports, where a mist bind failure takes down the whole runner rather than failing one test. The two bugs are coupled the opposite way round from the original body.

The original CONCLUSION survives: two symptoms, one cause. The incident in agents/Rowan.md where a fixture deleted a live proof is verify_test.gleam:34 simplifile.delete(path). Same cause, just not the one that was named.

FIX. verify_test cannot move off the live checkout: lake build Rule30.Proofs.X needs the file inside the project, and the built .lake is a real 7.4 GB constraint rather than an accident. So make the write survivable instead of relocating it -- a probe name nothing in the DAG can ever claim, asserted at test time, so a crash between write and delete leaves litter rather than eating a proof. Litter is a cleanup; a deleted proof is a node that silently reopens.

SAME PASS, LATENT RATHER THAN OBSERVED: test/dispatch_test.gleam:27 cfg_for overrides dag_path, runs_root, roster_path and agents_dir but NOT bugs_path, which stays pointed at the live board. Nothing writes today, because every prove_one call at lines 129-154 asserts Error. The first dispatch_test that completes an attempt files onto the real board. One line. Labelled latent on purpose -- not repeating the mistake this correction is about.

RULING 2026-09-06, Keel, asked for by Rowan. STAYS OPEN.

Fathom flagged this closable against 44c1792 and called it Keel's. It is not
closable, for a reason the bug's own body already contains: 44c1792 makes the
fixture's node id unable to collide with a real node's file, which downgrades
the worst case from LOSING A PROOF to LEAVING LITTER. Real, and worth having.
But the write into the live checkout still happens, and CLAUDE.md's stated test
for this bug being fixed is that HARNESS_REPO_ROOT stops being needed.
verify_test.gleam:30 still defaults to C:\Users\dibuj\dev\rule30 when the
variable is unset, so the test is not met.

Rowan reached this independently before asking, and Fathom reached it
independently again after checking main:verify_test.gleam and before reading
Keel's answer. Three of us agreeing is only evidence because two of those three
did not agree by talking.

COUPLING, Fathom's, and it is the useful part. 44c1792's own docstring says the
remaining hazard is a runner killed between the write and the delete. That is
the same failure mode as `a-green-suite-can-under-report-and-still-look-green`
-- a runner that dies mid-suite. So a completeness check that makes a killed
runner loud also makes this litter attributable instead of mysterious, and the
two should be read together rather than closed separately.

NARROWED 2026-09-06 by Keel. The concurrency case that briefly lived here has
moved to its own entry, `two-suites-share-one-fixture-path-in-the-live-checkout`,
on Fathom's argument that this bug's premise is ONE RUNNER KILLED MID-TEST and
that one is TWO HEALTHY RUNNERS. Different premise, different fix, different
closure test.

What stays here, because it is a correction to this entry rather than a separate
defect: the docstring this bug rests on (verify_test.gleam:9-13) said "a runner
killed between the write and the delete", singular, and never said it assumed
one. Two of three people who looked at a leftover fixture file reasoned from it
and got the wrong cause. The docstring is now explicit about what it assumes.

THIS BUG IS UNCHANGED AND STILL OPEN. Severity stays `friction`: the collision
was the reason to consider `blocks` and it is no longer this entry's problem.
CLAUDE.md's stated closure test is that HARNESS_REPO_ROOT stops being needed,
and verify_test.gleam:30 still defaults to the live checkout.

bugs.title: Guard tests bind fixed ports and a bind failure kills the whole runner
bugs.body:
Three independent sightings in one night: Rowan's first `gleam test` in a worktree died with a supervisor kill at the same minute another suite ran in the main checkout; a transient Eaddrinuse appeared during the Task 0 run from a just-exited process; and again during the Task 1 fix round.

The guard tests bind fixed ports, and mist's bind failure takes the whole test runner down rather than failing one test. So a stray `erl` from a previous run, or a second checkout running its suite, turns into a total and confusingly-attributed failure.

Two candidate fixes were discussed. Keel and Rowan both prefer picking ports from a free range at test time over a one-suite-at-a-time rule: the rule is unenforceable across two checkouts, which is exactly how it was hit. A bind failure should also fail its own test rather than the runner.
bugs.resolution: Fixed by Fathom in 2f205b8, landed in main at 3613177. harness_ffi.erl gains free_port_span/1: the OS picks a starting hint and the span is checked by binding every port in it and closing them again. A span rather than a single port because dispatch advances next_port by one per attempt, so a run fixture needs a contiguous range and an OS-assigned ephemeral port says nothing about its neighbours. The suite now binds no fixed port anywhere: guard_test no longer takes 4130, and run_test no longer takes 4231/4241/4251/4252/4261. Note that 8de1ec3 claimed guard_test held the only real bind; that claim is false and was superseded by 3ee9a62 -- run_test held five more, and the larger exposure was the one the first commit did not fix. Evidence, from Fathom: before, holding 127.0.0.1:4231 alone gave "106 passed, 3 failures" with run_test dead as a module and 75 tests never run against a true total of 181; after, holding all six formerly-bound ports at once gave 181 passed, no failures. Verified independently by Rowan on the merged tree at 3613177: 191 passed, no failures (191 rather than 181 because keel/test-isolation adds seed_test.gleam in the same landing). The under-reporting this exposed -- a killed runner still printing a plausible count in the right format -- is a separate defect and is being filed on its own by Fathom; it is not closed by this fix.

bugs.title: hit_ceiling ignores a refusal that arrives below the utilization ceiling
bugs.body:
Found by the Task 0 reviewer while checking the fix for hit-ceiling-misreads-allowed-warning.

hit_ceiling gates on `utilization >=. ceiling && !starts_with(status, "allowed")`. A rate_limit_event carrying a genuinely refusing status at, say, 0.5 utilization therefore returns False and the window is treated as open. This preserves the behaviour that existed before that fix and the conjunction was deliberate, so it is not a regression â€” but it is the opposite misread living in the same predicate: the fixed bug over-parked on a warning, this one under-parks on a refusal.

Filed rather than fixed because the reviewer's advice was a board line, not a code change in that task, and because nobody has yet seen a refusing status below the ceiling in the wild. Decide it with evidence: check whether the API ever sends one.

bugs.title: Line-ending churn reports untouched files as modified
bugs.body:
Seven files Rowan committed with LF show as modified in a Windows checkout the moment anything touches them, with `git diff --numstat` reporting zero changed lines. They are stat-dirty, not different.

The cost is not the churn itself, it is that it disguises real changes. Mid-plan this looked like another session had written into the checkout, which is a serious thing to see, and it took a numstat to rule out. Agents are told to stage explicit paths and read `git diff --cached` precisely so unrelated work is not swept into a commit; that discipline is much harder when seven unrelated files are permanently listed as modified.

The fix is a `.gitattributes` pinning `eol=lf`, which Rowan identified in its notebook and correctly flagged as Dib's call rather than an agent's. Do not commit the churned files as a workaround: they have no content diff, so staging them would bake CRLF line endings into the repository instead.

WORKAROUND, found 2026-09-06 by Keel, which makes this survivable without
touching the 32 files. `gleam format --check src test` in a fresh worktree
reports EVERY file as unformatted, so it cannot tell you whether your own change
drifted -- the signal is entirely swamped. To check one file for real drift,
compare it against its own formatting with the line endings normalised out:

  tr -d '\r' < f > /tmp/o && gleam format --stdin < /tmp/o | diff /tmp/o -

Empty diff means the file is correctly formatted and the --check failure is
purely CRLF. This does not fix the bug; it makes the formatter usable as a check
again, which was the part that actually hurt.

bugs.title: A wall node that becomes an open leaf aborts the whole run
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, after seeding the DAG's first `wall` node (evolve_left_diagonals_isEventuallyPeriodic) on 2026-09-06.

`schedule.next_to_start` has no `Wall` case: it ranks a wall node like any other open leaf once its deps are proved. `dispatch.start` then calls `config.model_for(Wall, _)`, whose ladder is empty by design, and returns Error("ladder exhausted for `X` although it is an open leaf"). `fill` propagates that Error, so the whole run aborts â€” not just that node â€” and it will abort again on every subsequent run, because nothing marks the node unselectable. The message's own wording ("although it is an open leaf") shows the author expected this to be unreachable.

The spec is clear that wall means "do not attempt without decomposing", so the fix belongs in the scheduler, not in dispatch: a wall node is not an open leaf, because an open leaf is a task the scheduler can actually start. Right fix is a `Wall` case in `next_to_start` that filters it out, with a test that a wall leaf is skipped and the run continues to the next candidate.

Not yet reachable in practice: the wall node's deps are three unproved nodes deep. It becomes live the moment that tier closes.
bugs.resolution: Fixed in the scheduler, not dispatch: next_to_start now filters Wall out of its candidates and returns None when only walled leaves remain, so a run with nothing startable ends cleanly instead of erroring out of fill. dag.open_leaves is deliberately unchanged -- a walled node's deps really are satisfied, and that is a DAG fact rather than a scheduling decision. `status` gained a separate "Walled leaves, ready but never dispatched" section so it stops presenting them as dispatchable, and dispatch.start's unreachable "although it is an open leaf" text was replaced with one that is true. Verified by Rowan independently from a re-pointed worktree as well as by review; commit bdddd8f.

bugs.title: Long node ids run into the status column in `gleam run -- status`
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan on 2026-09-06.

The status table pads the id column to a fixed width, and the new diagonal nodes are longer than it. The line reads

  evolve_left_fourth_diagonal_isEventuallyPeriodicopen      S     P1

with the id and the status fused. Cosmetic, and only in the human-facing table â€” the DAG itself is fine â€” but `status` is the command a human reads to decide what to dispatch, so it is the one place the board should stay legible. Pad to the longest id present rather than to a constant.
bugs.resolution: Fixed in the same commit as the wall-node bug, because it is the same rendering code and doing it separately would have meant editing that function twice. The id column now pads to the longest id actually present rather than a constant, generalised rather than widened to fit the one known offender, with a test using a 48-character id; commit bdddd8f.

bugs.title: A guard event says a command was denied but not which command
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, 2026-09-06, run 20260906T150452Z. Filed as a second sighting of guard-events-carry-no-node first, which was wrong twice over: that bug was already fixed in 0451d47, and my run was driven from a worktree pinned at 54d2f2b, so what I saw was the pre-fix code. The observation below is what survives once that is stripped out, and it is a different defect.

guard.event_fields logs node, event, tool and decision. 0451d47 added the node, which settles attribution. What is still absent is the command. A Deny therefore reads as `tool: Bash, decision: Deny(only 'lake build [modules]' and 'lake env lean <file>' are permitted...)` and never says what the worker actually tried to run.

Why that matters more than attribution did. The denial message names the rule, so a reader knows which rule fired, but not whether it should have: a worker reaching for `lake build --help` and a worker reaching for `rm -rf` produce byte-identical events. Deciding whether the guard is correctly tight or wrongly tight is exactly the judgement this project needs the log for, and that judgement needs the command.

It is also unrecoverable from anywhere else, which is the part that makes it worth fixing rather than working around. An *allowed* command survives in the turn-end stream events: the full `lake build Rule30.Proofs.EvolveRightEdge` appears five times in run 20260906T144745Z's record. A *denied* one is refused at PreToolUse, so no tool_use is ever emitted and nothing reaches the stream. The guard is the only component that sees the command at the moment it is refused, so the guard event is the only place it can be recorded.

Same dependent as the bug it came from: a bug auto-filed from a denial would carry no content to act on and no signature to dedupe two different denials apart.

Note for whoever fixes it: the command can carry secrets in general, though not under this grammar, which permits only lake invocations. Worth a moment's thought before logging it verbatim, not a reason to skip it.
bugs.resolution: event_fields now carries `attempted` (the command for Bash, the path for a write, capped at 400 chars inside event_fields rather than at the producer, so the cap is a property of the row) and `denial` (a stable slug from the new Denial type). Commit 4a4c2e6, in main at e413c8c. A denial row now says what was refused and whether retrying could ever work.

bugs.title: A non-array bugs field still costs the whole report
bugs.body:
Found by the reviewer of Task 5 round 2, and deliberately left open rather than fixed in that round.

The promise the bug-reporting channel is built on: nothing a worker puts in `bugs` may ever cost the turn's proof outcome. Two rounds closed the per-element routes -- the array is now read as `decode.list(decode.dynamic)` and each element decoded independently with `list.filter_map`, so a malformed or wrong-typed entry is discarded and `outcome`, `notebook` and `journal` survive.

One route remains. If `bugs` is present but is not an array at all -- a string, an object -- then `decode.list(decode.dynamic)` itself fails, and that failure is not per-element, so it threads up and fails the whole `Report` decode. The proof outcome is lost exactly as in the original incident.

Probability is low: constrained decoding should produce an array or nothing. But `posts-required-in-schema-not-in-decoder` is the proof that 'should' is not 'does', and it cost a correct proof.

Fix: give the array decode a fallback so a non-array `bugs` degrades to an empty list rather than failing -- the same treatment the field already gets when absent. Small. Left for the quiet window because a live run was in flight and this needs the test suite.
bugs.resolution: worker.gleam's report decoder reads `bugs` through `dynamic_list` -- an array of undecoded values, or [] when the field is not an array -- and decodes each element with list.filter_map. A field written in the wrong shape now degrades to "not supplied", the answer it already got when absent, instead of failing the whole Report and discarding the outcome. Commit 3b4b867, in main at 7c80082. Four tests, each watched failing first. SUCCESSOR FILED DELIBERATELY: `a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace` -- this fix trades a loud catastrophic loss for a silent small one, and the silence is a second problem rather than an acceptable price.

bugs.title: A bug left claimed by a dead session has no way back
bugs.body:
Noticed while Rowan was fixing the same shape in agents/sessions.json, and it is inherited rather than invented: the board borrows dag.json's status vocabulary on purpose, `claimed` included, so that the one board idiom transfers.

It transferred the hazard too. The DAG has the same problem -- a dispatcher that crashes mid-attempt leaves a node `claimed` -- and the harness answers it with an explicit `reopen` command that refuses any status but `claimed`. The bug board has no equivalent. A Keel session that claims a bug and is then killed, times out, or exhausts its context leaves that bug claimed forever, and nothing will ever un-claim it.

Rowan's framing of the same class, which is the clearest statement of it: a contract whose correctness depends on graceful shutdown is a contract that will not hold, because agent sessions almost never shut down gracefully.

Not yet biting: nothing on the board is claimed, and there is one maintainer. It starts biting the moment claiming is used at all.

Two candidate fixes, and the second is probably right. Either add a `reopen` for bugs, mirroring the DAG's; or drop `claimed` from the board's statuses entirely, since with a single maintainer it conveys nothing that `open` plus a look at git does not. The second removes the hazard instead of managing it, at the cost of the idiom being slightly less parallel to the DAG.

bugs.title: A build lock timeout reaches the worker as a Deny, indistinguishable in kind from a forbidden command
bugs.body:
Observed live by Rowan in run 20260906T150452Z at concurrency 2.

Cadence, proving evolve_left_fifth_diagonal, ran `lake build` at 15:26:46Z while Vesper held the build lock, and got:

  {"tool":"Bash","decision":"Deny(build lock timeout)"}

The safety property is right and should not change: an AcquireBuild that times out must become a Deny, so a worker never proceeds believing it holds a lock it does not. The friction is what the worker is told.

A worker's brief says the only two commands it may run are `lake build` and `lake env lean`. So the one command it is explicitly permitted comes back denied, and the text is diagnostic rather than actionable â€” it names the internal condition, not the response. Nothing in it says the denial is transient, that another worker caused it, or that retrying is the correct move. A worker could reasonably read it as 'building is refused' and either abandon the node or thrash against a rule it cannot satisfy. It is the same message shape as the grammar denial, which is genuinely permanent and must not be retried.

Cadence recovered on its own â€” it retried and got AcquireBuild at 15:30:37Z â€” so this cost about four minutes rather than the node. That is the good case, not the guaranteed one, and the cost scales with concurrency: one build lock shared by three workers makes this the normal path rather than the unlucky one.

Suggested fix is the wording, not the mechanism: say that another worker holds the build lock and that the right move is to wait and run the same command again. A denial a worker can act on correctly is worth more than one that accurately names an internal state.

---

Keel's amendment, and it supersedes the fix suggested above.

**The fix is structural, not wording.** `Decision` currently has one `Deny(reason: String)` carrying every refusal, so "you may never do this" and "not right now" are the same value with different prose. That is why the two are indistinguishable to a worker â€” they are literally the same case, and no wording can separate them for long. The next person to add a third kind of refusal puts it in the same variant and the bug returns wearing new text.

Split the variant instead: a `Busy` (or `DenyTransient`) alongside `Deny`, with the message generated per case rather than passed in. The hook protocol only offers allow/deny at the wire, so a worker still sees a denial either way, but the Gleam type then makes it impossible to emit a transient refusal that reads like a permanent one. `event_fields` can also log which kind it was, which is what guard-events-do-not-record-the-denied-command wants for a different reason.

The safety property is untouched: a timed-out AcquireBuild still denies, because a worker proceeding while it believes it holds a lock it does not is the failure worth keeping.

**The text should still change, and say what to do rather than what happened.** "Another worker holds the build lock; wait a few seconds and run the same command again" is actionable. "build lock timeout" is a diagnosis addressed to whoever wrote the harness, which is the wrong audience â€” the reader is a worker with exactly two permitted commands, one of which just failed.

**The scaling argument is the reason to fix this, not the incident.** The incident came out fine: Cadence recovered in four minutes. One lock shared by three workers makes contention the normal path rather than the unlucky one, and a worker that reads a transient refusal as permanent abandons a node it could have proved. Abandonment is expensive and quiet â€” it costs a full attempt off the ladder and looks like a hard node rather than a harness defect, so it would be miscounted as difficulty in the calibration data as well.

REOPENED 2026-09-06 by Keel. Rowan closed this `wontfix` on the reasoning that a
lock timeout reaching a worker as a `Deny` is indistinguishable IN KIND from a
policy refusal. That half stands and is not being relitigated: a worker cannot
act on the distinction, so the worker-facing message stays as it is.

WHAT DEFEATS THE RULING IS NOT THE FREQUENCY. Rowan's own correction, and it
sharpens the entry: a build lock timeout is A SECOND CAUSE WITH ITS OWN REMEDY,
merged into a signature built for the first. A grammar refusal means the brief
did not land and the fix is the brief. A lock timeout means a sibling worker held
the lock, the command was legal, and the fix is in the scheduler or the lock --
nothing about the worker, the brief or the allowlist. Two causes needing opposite
responses cannot share one bug, and that is true whether it happens nine times or
once.

THE COUNT IS WHAT MADE ANYONE LOOK, and it is worth recording as evidence rather
than as the argument. Every guard denial in the project's history, decoded per
line across all five runs in `runs/`:

    25 denial occurrences (23 distinct; two are genuine same-second retries)
    15  bash_grammar   60%
     9  lock_timeout   36%
     1  write_path      4%

Lock contention is the second most common thing the guard does, and the original
ruling was made without a number. But a rarer second cause would have deserved
reopening just as much -- the first wording of this reopening implied otherwise
and was wrong.

WHAT IS ALSO NEW: THE RECORD SIDE IS DISTINGUISHABLE EVEN THOUGH THE WORKER SIDE
IS NOT, which did not exist when the ruling was made. 4a4c2e6 splits `Deny` into
`kind` (for the record) and `reason` (for the worker), so the two halves can be
answered separately and the record can name the cause without changing anything
the worker sees.

PROVENANCE, because it matters here. Fathom computed a tally, said plainly that
its own classifier and denominator could be wrong in a way nothing downstream
would catch, and asked to be re-run rather than believed. Keel re-ran it with a
deliberately wider filter. Fathom's lock count of 9 was exactly right. Its total
of 21 was low, and its two-way classifier folded a write-path denial into
`grammar`, which is how a third cause stayed invisible in both our numbers. The
reopening rests on the re-run, not on the first tally.

bugs.title: An attempt the harness broke is scored as a hard node
bugs.body:
Observed by Rowan while filing build-lock-timeout-reads-as-a-permission-refusal, filed by Keel as the general case rather than the instance.

When a harness defect causes a worker to abandon, nothing distinguishes that from the node being hard. The attempt is recorded with outcome `abandoned`, it consumes a rung of the model ladder, and it lands in the size-calibration data as evidence of difficulty. So a harness bug does not merely cost one proof: it silently corrupts the signal the overseer uses to price every future node, and it does so in the direction that makes the node look worse than it is. The next dispatch at that node starts on a more expensive model for no reason.

Rowan's point, and it is the part that would take a long time to see from outside: this is invisible precisely because the record looks correct. An abandoned attempt is a normal thing. Nothing in the DAG says why.

The signal now exists and is unused. Since provers can file bugs in their end-of-turn report, an attempt that both abandoned AND filed a `blocks`-severity bug is very likely a harness failure rather than a hard node. Nothing correlates the two.

Candidate fixes, cheapest first. Record on the `Attempt` whether the worker filed a blocking bug, and exclude those attempts from calibration and from the ladder count -- an attempt the harness broke should not spend a rung. Or add an outcome distinct from `abandoned` for it. The first is smaller and uses data already being collected as of the bug-reporting channel.

Worth doing before the calibration numbers are trusted for anything, because the corruption is retroactive: the attempts already on the board cannot be re-scored.

--- AMENDED after Rowan refuted the proposed heuristic ---

The 'abandoned AND filed a blocks bug' correlation above is kept only as a weak secondary signal, because it misses the exact case that motivated this entry.

Rowan's objection, which is correct: a worker that receives Deny("build lock timeout"), reads it as a permanent rule, and gives up DOES NOT FILE A BUG. It has no complaint. It believes it hit a legitimate boundary and behaved correctly. The workers who file blocking bugs are the ones who noticed something was wrong, and a worker defeated by a harness defect it mistook for a rule is by definition one that did not notice. So the correlation is blind precisely where it is needed.

The inverse fails too, less badly: a worker can file a genuine blocks bug and still be beaten by a genuinely hard node, and excluding that attempt discards a real difficulty signal.

Better primary signal, and it needs the Decision split from build-lock-timeout-reads-as-a-permission-refusal: once the guard distinguishes transient from permanent refusals and event_fields logs which kind, the harness can observe 'this attempt received transient denials and then abandoned' without asking the worker anything. That is derived from outside the process by the component that actually knows. The guard is a reliable witness; a worker is not, especially about a failure it did not perceive as one.

This is the same principle Rowan and Keel arrived at independently earlier the same day, in agents/sessions.json and in the board's `claimed` status: where state must survive a session that dies without warning, derive it from outside the process rather than asking the process to report it.

Plan: guard-derived signal primary, filed-bug correlation secondary. Two weak signals failing in different directions beat one that fails in the direction that matters. This makes the Decision variant split load-bearing for three separate entries, which is an argument for doing it first.

Ownership, settled with Rowan: calibration is not separable from this. calibration_hits/calibration_total live in roster.gleam and the ladder count is failed_attempts in dispatch.gleam, both in harness/. Splitting it would put two agents in one area on one coherent change. Keel takes Attempt, failed_attempts and the roster calibration together; Rowan reviews whether the resulting numbers mean what the overseer needs them to mean.

RETROACTIVE, and not fixable: every attempt already recorded was scored under this defect, so the calibration figures quoted in agents/Rowan.md -- Vesper 2/3, and the five attempts of 2026-09-06 -- are contaminated to an unknown degree. Nobody is going to re-score them. Written down here so the first person to trust those numbers knows they predate the fix.

bugs.title: Nothing tells a session whether uncommitted work is live or orphaned
bugs.body:
Near-miss on 2026-09-06, no loss. Reported jointly: Keel found it, Rowan supplied the analysis that makes it a real bug rather than an anecdote.

WHAT HAPPENED. Keel found 192 uncommitted lines across all 14 files in Rule30/Proofs/ -- teaching docstrings, real work, existing in exactly one place. ListAgents showed two sessions that had been live forty minutes earlier were gone. Keel concluded the work might be orphaned by a dead session and stopped rather than tidying. It was in fact Rowan's, mid-verification.

THE DEFECT IS NOT THE WRONG CONCLUSION, IT IS THAT THE EVIDENCE CANNOT SUPPORT A RIGHT ONE. Rowan's framing: the two vanished sessions really were its provers, they really had ended, and a reader with only that evidence could not distinguish in-progress work from abandoned work. The shared checkout cannot tell 'being written' from 'left behind', and neither can any observer. `git status` shows that uncommitted work exists; nothing shows whose it is or how old it is.

WHY THE WINDOW EXISTS, AND WHY 'JUST COMMIT PROMPTLY' IS NOT THE FIX. Rowan's work sat uncommitted for about twenty minutes because it was running `lake build` between editing and committing. That is not carelessness, it is the verification step this project requires -- no agent, including the dispatcher, gets to declare a proof done by assertion. Any fix premised on committing sooner is asking people to commit unverified work, which is the one thing the project explicitly refuses. That tension is the actual content of this bug.

AUTO-COMMIT IS PROBABLY THE WRONG FIX, and both of us independently landed there. Half-finished work committed automatically now auto-pushes to a branch on a public remote under whatever identity is configured, which is worse than losing it.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY HELP is visibility rather than automation: something a session can consult to see uncommitted work it did not write, and how long it has been sitting. The first half exists in `git status`; the second half -- attribution and age -- does not exist anywhere. A session starting work in this checkout currently has no way to know it is about to step on someone.

THE MITIGATION THAT ACTUALLY WORKED, and it is worth keeping regardless of any fix: every implementer dispatched into this checkout is instructed to stage explicit paths only, and never to run `git add -A`, `git add .`, `git checkout` or `git restore` on any path. That discipline is what protected these 14 files while three agents worked around them.

RELATED: this is the other half of the problem Rowan fixed in agents/sessions.json. That fix removed the stale-row hazard -- state a dead session leaves behind that misleads a reader. This is the same class one layer down, and larger: state a dead session leaves behind that a reader cannot even classify.

bugs.title: Seeding is the one step with no agent and no adjudicator
bugs.body:
DESIGN BRIEF, not a defect report. Filed by Rowan with Dib's rulings attached, so
Keel can build this without re-running the brainstorm.

THE GAP. The project's governing principle is that no agent declares a proof done
by assertion: `lake build` adjudicates every proof from outside the session that
wrote it. THERE IS NO EQUIVALENT ON THE STATEMENT SIDE. Every one of the 15 nodes
in dag.json is true because a captain checked it by hand and said so.

WHY THAT IS EXPENSIVE RATHER THAN MERELY UNTIDY. A false seed lemma never fails.
It sits on the board, consumes attempt after attempt, escalates haiku -> sonnet ->
opus, and is INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GENUINELY HARD NODE. Every signal the fleet
produces about it -- attempt count, escalation, cost -- reads as difficulty. The
board has no state that means "this cannot be proved because it is not true".
Today that is survivable because seeding is one careful captain doing #eval
cross-checks by hand at a rate of one tier per day. It stops being survivable at
the moment seeding is delegated or automated, which is exactly what this ticket
asks for. THE CHECK MUST LAND BEFORE OR WITH THE ROLE, NOT AFTER IT.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW. Seeding is the only step in the loop with no name attached.
Provers prove, Rowan dispatches, Keel fixes the machinery, Cairn explains; the
captain pass has no agent and no automation, which is why it is the step that ran
dry this morning at 14 of 15 with an empty dispatchable frontier. It will run dry
again at every tier boundary. Rowan seeded the next tier by hand today rather than
block the fleet on this ticket -- that is a workaround, and it is the same
workaround every time.

DIB'S RULINGS (2026-09-06). Two, both settled, neither to be relitigated:

1. A SEEDER PROPOSES; ROWAN REVIEWS AND LANDS. The seeder never writes
   Rule30/Statements.lean or blueprint/dag.json -- the two files the whole fleet
   reads and workers are forbidden to touch. Its output is a proposal artifact.
   Rationale: seeding sets direction, and direction should not change while nobody
   is watching. Same class of ruling as one-session-per-persona.

2. GUARD ALLOWLIST: the seeder MAY create and run scripts under explorer/, and
   nothing outside it. Rejected as too tight: existing scripts only -- this
   morning's one good idea (the diagonal recurrence, which later proofs cited
   instead of re-deriving the coordinate shift) came out of
   explorer/diagonalscan.mjs, a file that did not exist when the pass began.
   Rejected as too clumsy: Lean #eval only, no JS -- correct against the real
   definitions, unusable for scanning 63 diagonals to N=16000.
   NOTE HONESTLY WHAT THIS BUYS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. `node` on a file the agent
   just authored is a shell wearing a hat. The directory fence is a real bound on
   what gets WRITTEN and a thin one on what gets RUN. This is a wider trust
   surface than any prover has, granted deliberately, with Dib's eyes open. It is
   not a precedent for widening the prover allowlist -- different role, different
   list, and the standing rule that loosening the guard is never a fix on its own
   is untouched.

SHAPE (Rowan's sketch, Keel owns the design).
- `gleam run -- seed`, hand-started like Keel and unlike a prover. Not
  scheduler-triggered: an empty board should report itself, not reseed itself.
- The brief is where the quality lives, and it is the part worth spending on. The
  seeding that worked this morning worked because the captain had read every proof
  and knew which shapes closed cheaply. A fresh session has none of that unless
  the brief carries it: the closed-node table with sizes/models/costs, the /-! notes
  from Rule30/Proofs/, explorer/README.md, and the wall-node convention.
- Output: a proposal file (statements + proposed dag nodes + deps + size estimates),
  written somewhere Rowan reads and the fleet does not.
- The harness runs the statement check over the proposal BEFORE Rowan reads it, so
  review starts from checked claims.

THE CHECK, AND ITS HONEST LIMIT. A statement here is universally quantified
(`forall t, evolve (t+3) (-(t:Z)) = decide (t % 2 = 0)`), so a mechanical check can
only instantiate over a finite range. Some seeded statements are not testable that
way at all -- IsEventuallyPeriodic carries an existential, the density lemmas are
about reals. So proposed shape: EVERY PROPOSED NODE CARRIES A FALSIFICATION
WITNESS -- a Lean #eval-able Bool-valued expression over an explicit finite range,
run by `lake env lean` on a scratch file, with the range recorded on the node the
way `verified` is recorded. A node whose claim cannot be written that way is
admitted as `unchecked` and needs Rowan's explicit sign-off. That is partial
coverage stated plainly rather than pretended, and it puts the burden of
falsifiability on the seeder, which is the discipline the role most needs.

Run it in Lean, not only in the JS engine. The engine is a second implementation;
#eval is the definition the theorem is actually about, and a mirrored coordinate
convention would make the engine agree with a wrong statement. Cross-checking both
is better still: disagreement between them is itself a finding.

FIRST TEST, FREE. Run the check against the 15 nodes already on the board. They
are all believed true, so anything it flags is a bug in the check -- a calibration
run that costs no subscription and no seeding pass.

ONE THING THAT DOES NOT WORK, SO NOBODY SPENDS A DAY ON IT. A seeder cannot be
scored the way a prover is. A prover has a crisp success signal (build green,
axioms clean) available at the end of its own session. A seeded node is good only
in retrospect -- when it closes cheaply and gets cited by the proofs after it. Any
design that tries to close a seeding attempt with an outcome verdict at session end
is inventing a signal that does not exist. Derive seeding quality later, from what
happened to the nodes, the same way calibration is derived from closed attempts.

MEASURED 2026-09-06 by Keel, before building the witness, and it changes what the
witness can be. The ticket proposes "a Lean #eval-able Bool-valued expression over
an explicit finite range" and treats the range as a free parameter. IT IS NOT
FREE. `evolve t = rule30^[t] initialConfig` over `Config := Int -> Bool`, so
evaluating one cell at depth t costs 3^t neighbour evaluations. Timed against the
real definitions with `lake env lean`, on the true statement
`(List.range n).all (fun t => evolve t (-(t:Int)) == true)`:

    n = 12     3.2s     (all of it Lean startup)
    n = 14     3.8s
    n = 16    12.3s
    n = 18    84.4s
    n = 20    timeout at 120s

SO THE USABLE RANGE IS ABOUT t < 18, AND THE WALL IS SHEER. Two steps buys you a
factor of seven. Any node whose claim only becomes interesting past t = 18 cannot
carry a naive witness at all, and that includes most of what the board will want
to say about periodicity.

AND THERE IS AN ASYMMETRY THAT HAS TO BE DESIGNED FOR, not discovered later.
`List.all` short-circuits, so A FALSE WITNESS RETURNS ALMOST INSTANTLY AND A TRUE
ONE PAYS THE FULL EXPONENTIAL. That is operationally good -- finding a falsehood
is the cheap case -- but it makes a timeout AMBIGUOUS in exactly the direction
that matters: a witness that times out has NOT been shown true, and must be
recorded as `unchecked`, never as a pass. A checker that treats "no falsification
found before the deadline" as success would pass every statement too expensive to
check, which is the class most likely to be wrong.

I NEARLY MISMEASURED THIS, and the way I nearly did is the reason the numbers are
worth trusting. My first timing run used a FALSE predicate, got a flat 3.1s across
n = 8..16, and read it as "evaluation is free". It was `List.all` bailing at the
first counterexample. A timing measurement that cannot distinguish "fast" from
"stopped early" is the same defect as a check that cannot return no. The numbers
above are from a predicate that is true across the whole range, so every element
was actually evaluated.

THIRD THING THE TICKET GETS RIGHT AND SHOULD KEEP: `#eval false` EXITS 0. Verified.
A witness checker built on exit status would pass every false statement silently.
The verdict must be parsed from stdout, and anything that is neither exactly
`true` nor exactly `false` is a broken check rather than a falsified statement --
the two mean opposite things and must not share a verdict.

bugs.title: Nothing checks that a bug's premise is true before a fix is planned
bugs.body:
guard-events-carry-no-node claimed that under --concurrency 3 all three guards write to one runs/<id>/events.jsonl. They do not, and had not since 68ae08b -- every attempt gets its own directory and its own log. I filed that bug, planned Task 4 around it, implemented it, reviewed it, and wrote the false claim into three doc comments, and it survived all of that because a bug body is prose that nobody adjudicates.

This is the statement-side gap that seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role describes, in a second place. A proof is adjudicated by lake build from outside the session that wrote it. A bug report is adjudicated by nobody, and a false one is indistinguishable from a true one -- it consumes a task, ships code, and leaves comments behind that are worse than no comments.

Not proposing a mechanical checker: a bug body is not falsifiable the way a Lean statement is. The cheap version is a discipline with a place to record it -- a bug that asserts something about how the harness behaves today carries the file:line or commit that shows it, checked when the fix is planned rather than when the bug is filed. Filed as friction against my own process, not as a defect in the board's code.

UPDATED 2026-09-06 after four more instances in one day. THE CLASS HAS TWO SHAPES and lumping them loses the fix.

SHAPE A -- nothing was checked at all. This ticket original case (guard-events-carry-no-node); the offline-fixtures body, which named the wrong writer entirely; the CLAUDE.md paragraph whose stated reason for HARNESS_REPO_ROOT is not its reason, since verify_test ignores the variable. Fix as already stated: a claim about how the harness behaves today carries the file:line that shows it, checked when the fix is PLANNED.

SHAPE B -- something WAS checked, but not the thing that shipped. Rowan verified an example with a forall-bound f and seeded a theorem with f as a parameter, then told the worker by decide closes it. It does not. Shape A fix does nothing here: there was a real check and it could have been cited, and it was still the wrong object. Shape B is the worse one, because a claim with real verification behind it reads MORE authoritative than an unchecked one and is wrong anyway.

THE COMMON SHAPE IS NARROWER THAN PROSE NOBODY ADJUDICATES, and this is the useful version: A TRANSCRIPTION THAT WAS NEVER DIFFED AGAINST ITS ORIGINAL. All of them were a retyping. Including the fourth: while demonstrating this defect, Keel retyped a seeded statement into a scratch file with a changed import line, read the resulting failure as the peer route being wrong, and came within one message of sending that correction. The discipline failed in the hands of the person who had written it down ten minutes earlier, which is the argument for machinery over discipline.

MEASURED, from run 20260906T162411Z: the node whose description was checked closed on the first rung; the node whose description was not cost $0.97 across two attempts and a wasted rung. Description quality drove cost, not node difficulty. See seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role and docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-06-seeder-design.md, where the route check is specified as the mechanical form of this.

bugs.title: Guard denied Bash
bugs.body: The guard refused a Bash call during the attempt at bool_map_iterate_three. If the worker needed it, the allowlist is wrong; if it did not, the brief is.
bugs.resolution: SUPERSEDED by the Denial split, 4a4c2e6, in main at e413c8c, and answerable at last. Vesper's entry asked: if the worker needed the command the allowlist is wrong, and if it did not the brief is. THE ANSWER IS BOTH, because the entry merged two causes that need opposite responses -- which is the defect, not the ambiguity. Of the five denials behind this signature, four were build-lock timeouts (a sibling worker held the lock; the command was legal and the harness took four minutes of the attempt away and told the worker 'permission denied') and one was a genuine grammar refusal (the brief did not land). Today the same five would file as guard:Bash:build_lock_timeout x4 and guard:Bash:not_permitted x1, each carrying the command that was refused. COUNTED, and the count is the reason `build-lock-timeout-reads-as-a-permission-refusal` is reopened below.

bugs.title: The freeze list is maintained by hand, so it drifts behind the code
bugs.body:
A freeze list names the files that are unsafe to touch while a run is in flight. It is written by a human and it drifts, because what makes a file unsafe is WHO WRITES IT, and the writer set changes in the code without the list being told.

Two independent instances in one afternoon, both verified in the source rather than reported. blueprint/bugs.json became dispatcher-written when auto_file_signals landed (dispatch.gleam:1003 load, :1032 save); the freeze announced for run 20260906T162411Z named dispatch/guard/schedule and .claude/ and did not name the board. agents/roster.json is dispatcher-written on a mint (dispatch.gleam:832) and on a colour backfill (:884), both via roster.save, which rewrites the whole file from the Roster loaded at :200 — so a hand-added row arriving between that load and that save is silently gone. No freeze list has ever named roster.json.

In both cases the person maintaining the list was the person who added the writer. That is structural, not careless: the list and the code are separate artefacts and nothing forces them to agree. It is the same shape as the transcription failures filed under a-bugs-premise-is-never-checked-before-it-is-fixed, one level up — a copy that is never diffed against its original.

FIX: stop maintaining the list. The set of files the dispatcher writes is derivable from the code — dag.json, bugs.json, roster.json, agents/<Name>.md, Rule30/Proofs.lean, and the run directory. A `gleam run -- writes` that prints that set cannot drift behind the code the way a remembered list does. The harness can print the set of files it writes; a human cannot remember it.

Not the fix: adding roster.json to the freeze list. That closes this instance and leaves the mechanism, which is the thing that produced two instances in one day.

SEPARATE, related, deliberately not folded in: CLAUDE.md is read whole by brief.gleam:188 into every worker's appended system prompt at brief-build time. It has one writer, so there is no lost update, but an edit landing mid-run briefs two workers in one run from different documents with nothing in the record saying which. That is unreproducible rather than corrupt and wants its own ticket if anyone thinks it is worth one.
bugs.resolution: `gleam run -- writes` derives the list from harness/src at run time instead of remembering it, so a file that becomes dispatcher-written shows up on the next invocation without anyone updating anything. Commit 298e604. What stays hand-maintained is the mapping from a file to the NAMES of its writing functions, and that is covered by a second check, `unaccounted`, which reports a raw simplifile write in a module that declares none -- what a brand-new writer looks like on its first day. Fathom reports the check found a false positive in ITSELF on first run (writes.gleam names every write token as data, so the scanner scanned as an undeclared writer) and that three fixture tests exist whose job is to make the checks fail, because the real-source test would be equally green if `unaccounted` returned [] unconditionally.

bugs.title: A worker can be told anything by any session, and the attempt record does not show it
bugs.body:
Demonstrated accidentally on 2026-09-06 at about 17:00Z. Not theorised.

WHAT HAPPENED. Keel misread the session list, believed rule30-19 was a newly-started framework colleague, and sent it a long welcome covering the freeze, worktree rules, gleam test hazards and guard internals. rule30-19 was Vesper on bool_driven_eventually_two_periodic, dispatched 16:57:27 -- the hardest node in the tier, mid-attempt. Retracted within minutes.

THE HOLE, in Rowan wording, which is the sharp one: THE GUARD IS A PreToolUse HOOK, SO IT CAN ONLY EVER SEE WHAT A WORKER DOES. IT STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE WHAT A WORKER IS TOLD. An inbound message is not a tool call, so this is not a gap that a wider or narrower allowlist could address -- it is a channel the mechanism is the wrong shape to observe.

VERIFIED BY ROWAN from the other side: runs/20260906T162411Z/bool_driven_eventually_two_periodic-1/events.jsonl holds exactly six events, one sent and five guard. ZERO TRACE OF THE MESSAGE. Not redacted, not unattributed -- the arrival is not an event at all. So the record is not merely incomplete, it is CONFIDENTLY COMPLETE AND WRONG.

WHY IT OUTRANKS THE THROUGHPUT BUGS (Rowan read, and Keel agrees). Every other entry on this board assumes an attempt record means what it says. An attempt outcome is read as evidence about the NODE, and that inference holds only if the attempt was isolated. Attempts are not isolated from the rest of the machine. A prover cannot distinguish a peer message from its dispatcher brief; both arrive as text, with no sender authority.

IT COST NOTHING THIS TIME. bool_driven_eventually_two_periodic closed on its first attempt, first rung, 14 turns, $0.64 -- the cheapest sonnet node in the tier bar one. Recorded because the finding does not depend on the damage: the record still would not have said why if it had gone the other way.

CANDIDATE FIXES, not chosen. Cheapest and probably right: log inbound peer messages into the attempt events.jsonl. It prevents nothing, but it restores attributability, which is what the board actually needs -- the same shape as the guard logging its denials. Stronger: quarantine inbound messages for the duration of an attempt, which has to be a property of the harness around the session rather than something the session enforces on itself.

CLAUDE.md says the trust boundary is the model plus the command allowlist. That sentence is now known to be incomplete, and it is the sentence the whole no-sandbox decision rests on. NEEDS DIB -- no agent should edit it unasked.

SAME FAMILY: harness-caused-abandonment-is-scored-as-difficulty and uncommitted-work-is-indistinguishable-from-abandoned-work. In each of them the record cannot express the thing you would need in order to interpret it.

bugs.title: A route checked against a paraphrase of the statement is worse than an unchecked one
bugs.body:
Observed by Rowan on 2026-09-06, cost $0.85 and a wasted ladder rung in run
20260906T162411Z. Filed about ninety minutes after filing
`seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role`, by the person who filed it, which is the
evidence rather than the embarrassment.

WHAT HAPPENED. The seeded statement was

  theorem bool_map_iterate_three (f : Bool -> Bool) : f^[3] = f

and its node description said, in the captain's voice, "`by decide` closes it,
which the captain confirmed before seeding." What the captain had actually run was

  example : forall f : Bool -> Bool, f^[3] = f := by decide

which does close. The seeded form does not: with `f` a parameter rather than
bound by `forall`, the goal carries a free variable and `decide` has nothing to
evaluate. Haiku spent 41 turns and $0.38 and died `budget_exhausted`; sonnet
closed it on the next rung for $0.59 by ignoring the route entirely.

TWO SHAPES, AND THIS IS THE WORSE ONE. Keel's framing, adopted:

  Shape A -- nothing was checked at all. `guard-events-carry-no-node`'s body,
  `offline-fixtures-write-into-the-live-checkout`'s body, the CLAUDE.md
  HARNESS_REPO_ROOT paragraph. Fixed by citing file:line when the fix is planned.

  Shape B -- something was checked, but not the thing that shipped. This one.
  Shape A's fix does nothing for it: there WAS a check, it COULD have been cited,
  and it was still the wrong object. Shape B is worse precisely because a claim
  with real verification behind it reads more authoritative than an unchecked one
  and is wrong anyway.

WHY THE FALSIFICATION WITNESS DOES NOT CATCH IT.
`seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role` proposes checking whether a seeded statement
is TRUE. This statement is true at every step. Nothing in that check would have
fired. The gap is a second one and it needs a second check.

THE FIX EXISTS ALREADY, ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BOARD, AND NOBODY NOTICED.
verify.gleam:76-86 does not trust a worker's transcription of a statement either:
it writes `theorem harness_check : type_of% Statements.<name> := <the worker's
theorem>` and elaborates that, so a proof is checked against the statement as it
exists in the file. That is exactly the shape-B guard, and it is why no worker in
this project has ever proved a subtly different theorem than the one it was given.
The captain has no equivalent, so a captain's scratch file and Statements.lean are
two unrelated texts that nothing cross-checks.

TWO AXES, AND THE NAIVE MECHANISM IS WRONG ON BOTH. Keel adjudicated this rather
than arguing it, in four lake env lean runs:

  1. DECLARATION TEXT, NOT TYPE. A check built on `type_of%` alone reproduces the
     bug: `type_of%` yields the forall-form, so `by decide` PASSES against it while
     failing in the worker's file where `f` is intro'd as a parameter. The check
     must elaborate the declaration text copied VERBATIM from the statement file,
     with the route substituted for `sorry`. `type_of%` keeps a job -- confirming
     that what you elaborated is the same theorem -- but it cannot be the first
     check.
  2. IMPORT ENVIRONMENT. The route also depends on ambient instances. The corrected
     route `revert f; decide` fails under `import Rule30.Basic` alone -- "failed to
     synthesize Decidable (forall f : Bool -> Bool, f^[3] = f)" -- and passes only
     with `Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi` or `Rule30.Prize`. `type_of%` checks import
     Rule30.Statements, which is strictly richer than any proof file's. So the check
     must run under a proof file's import list, not the statement file's.

Both failure messages point away from their real cause: the first names a binder
problem that reads like a tactic choice, the second names Decidable and reads like
the statement is undecidable rather than like an import is missing.

WHERE THE ROUTE SHOULD LIVE. Not in Rule30/Statements.lean, which is types. Not in
the node `description` string, which is where this one was and is exactly why
nothing could check it -- prose and claim are indistinguishable there. On the DAG
node as structured data, beside `size` and `deps`: `route: { tactics, imports } |
null`. `null` means the captain claims nothing, which is honest and strictly better
than prose asserting a route nobody ran.

AND THE MEASURED REASON THIS MATTERS LESS THAN IT LOOKS, WHICH CHANGES THE FIX.
The same run showed the route is the less valuable half of a description. The node's
English -- "the only four candidates are the identity, negation and the two
constants, and each is unchanged after three applications" -- is what sonnet
implemented, line for line, finding a better proof than either the captain's
original route or the captain's correction to it. Across the tier, both nodes whose
descriptions were verified closed on the first rung; the one that was not, did not.
Description quality dominated node difficulty as a cost driver, and it was not
close.

So the conclusion is not "check routes harder". It is: THE REASON IS REQUIRED AND
THE ROUTE IS OPTIONAL. An unverified route misdirects in the captain's voice to a
model with no standing to doubt it, and forecloses a search a stronger model would
win. A correct reason costs nothing and leaves the search open. A captain who
cannot state the reason has not finished thinking about the node; a captain who
cannot supply a route has merely left it open.

CALIBRATION SET, FREE AND AVAILABLE NOW. Do not calibrate a route check against the
fifteen previously closed nodes -- their routes are their proofs, every case passes
by construction, and a broken check looks identical to a working one. Use the five
descriptions seeded on 2026-09-06, which are a labelled set:
`isEventuallyPeriodic_shift` is a known positive (route correct, closed on haiku,
first rung) and `bool_map_iterate_three` is a known negative. A route check that
does not flag `by decide` on that statement is broken, and one run tells you.

bugs.title: A killed test runner still prints a plausible pass count
bugs.body:
A gleam test run that dies partway still prints a well-formed summary line, so a green-looking number is not evidence that the suite ran. Measured by Fathom on 2026-09-06 while fixing guard-tests-bind-fixed-ports: with 127.0.0.1:4231 held from outside, the suite printed "106 passed, 3 failures" with Exit(Shutdown(FailedToStartChild(0, InitFailed))) and Desc("module run_test") -- run_test had died as a module and 75 tests never ran at all, against a true total of 181. Nothing in the output distinguishes "ran and mostly passed" from "died a third of the way in". MECHANISM: mist.start builds a OneForOne supervisor and adds the glisten listener as a CHILD, so the bind happens inside child start and the supervisor is linked to the caller; FailedToStartChild takes the calling process down rather than returning through guard.start result.map_error. Confirmed from mist source and then observed. WHY THIS OUTLIVES THE PORTS FIX, which is why it is filed separately: 2f205b8 removes the specific trigger (no fixed ports remain) but not the failure mode. Any cause that kills the runner mid-suite -- not just a bind collision -- still yields a plausible count in the right format. The defect is that the runner has no completeness check: it reports what it got to, not what it was asked to do. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROJECT RECORD: every green suite cited as evidence before 2f205b8 was evidence only if nothing killed the runner partway, and the transcripts do not say. This is the same family as a `sorry` that still typechecks and as an attempt record that reads closed when it was contaminated -- the failure mode is a success report. SUGGESTED FIX: assert an expected total, or have the runner exit non-zero when the module count it completed is below the module count it discovered.

CORRECTED 2026-09-06 by Fathom, from a deliberate kill rather than an inference,
and written to the board by Keel, who holds this file. THE SUGGESTED FIX ABOVE
IS PARTLY WRONG.

It implies a shortfall measures the tests lost. It does not. EUnit reports each
cancellation as a failure, so the cancellations partly fill the hole they made:
a module of five tests cancelled at its first test printed `197 passed, 3
failures` against a 202 announced total -- a shortfall of 2 against a real loss
of 5. No denominator can do better, because the runner cannot know how many
tests were inside a module it never entered.

SO A SHORTFALL IS A LOWER BOUND, NOT A COUNT. The exact reading, and the only
one worth trusting, is the zero: a shortfall of zero means the suite ran whole.
That is what makes the fix worth having, and it is a narrower claim than the one
this entry was filed with.

Demonstrated rather than argued: a throwaway module whose first test starts a
second guard on a live port, which is the real mist mechanism -- a listener that
is a linked supervisor child, so the failed bind takes the calling process down
instead of returning an Error. Clean baseline immediately before and after, 197
expected and 197 passed, exit 0.

Fixed by suite_size.gleam plus harness_test.main. Sha pending: nobody is landing
tonight.
bugs.resolution: suite_size.gleam plus harness_test.main print the discovered total above every summary, so a run that lost a module to a killed runner no longer looks whole. Commit 4cbfba2, in main at e413c8c. Demonstrated under a real kill rather than argued, with the probe module removed afterwards so the baseline is not permanently changed. Note the correction already in this body: a shortfall is a LOWER BOUND on tests lost, not a count, because EUnit reports each cancellation as a failure. The exact reading is the zero.

bugs.title: A malformed posts entry fails the whole report and discards the outcome
bugs.body:
Found by Keel on 2026-09-06 while verifying the premise of its sibling
`a-non-array-bugs-field-still-poisons-the-report`, not by hitting it. Filed and
fixed in the same change; filed anyway, because the board is the record and a
defect that was never on it cannot be reasoned about later.

THE DEFECT. worker.gleam read `posts` as `decode.optional_field("posts", [],
decode.list(decode.string))`. That fails on a field that is not an array AND on
a well-formed array holding any single non-string element. Either failure
threads up through `optional_field` and fails the entire `Report`, so `outcome`,
`notebook` and `journal` are discarded with it. A worker that proved a theorem
and wrote one number into `posts` loses the proof.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE `bugs` ONE IT WAS FOUND BESIDE. Two rounds of work
removed exactly this per-element hazard from `bugs`, two lines below, and left
it standing in `posts`. So the sibling bug's own body understates the board:
`bugs` had one surviving route, per-field only, and its probability is genuinely
low because constrained decoding should emit an array or nothing. `posts` had
BOTH routes, and the per-element one is the likelier failure by a wide margin —
a list of mostly-strings with one wrong element is a shape a model produces far
more readily than a field of the wrong type outright.

AND IT HAS FIRED BEFORE, BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE. `posts-required-in-schema-not-in-
decoder` is the same field costing the same thing: Vesper proved
evolve_left_second_diagonal in one shot, omitted `posts`, and the turn became an
error. That was schema-vs-decoder disagreement rather than element typing, and
it cost a correct proof a re-dispatch. `posts` is now the only field on the
report that has destroyed an outcome twice, for two unrelated reasons.

FIX. Both fields now read through `dynamic_list` — an array of undecoded values,
or `[]` when the field is not an array — and decode element by element with
`list.filter_map`. A field written in the wrong shape degrades to "not
supplied", which is the answer it already got when absent.

Four tests, each watched failing first: non-array `bugs`, object-valued `bugs`,
non-array `posts`, and a well-formed `posts` array holding one number.

SUCCESSOR, DELIBERATE: `a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace`. The fix trades
a loud catastrophic loss for a silent small one, and the silence is a second
problem rather than an acceptable price.
bugs.resolution: Same commit and same mechanism as its sibling `a-non-array-bugs-field-still-poisons-the-report`: `posts` now goes through `dynamic_list` plus per-element filter_map, so neither a non-array field nor a single non-string element can cost the turn's outcome. Commit 3b4b867, in main at 7c80082. Two of the four new tests are this field's: a non-array `posts`, and a well-formed array holding one number -- the likelier shape, and the one `bugs` had been immune to for two rounds while `posts` was not.

bugs.title: A report field the decoder drops is not recorded anywhere
bugs.body:
Filed by Keel about its own fix, in the same change that created it. Rowan's
framing, which is the sharp one and is what prompted this entry.

WHAT THE FIX DID. `a-non-array-bugs-field-still-poisons-the-report` and
`a-malformed-posts-field-costs-the-proof-outcome` are both closed by making the
report's two optional array fields degrade instead of fail: a `bugs` or `posts`
entry the decoder cannot read is dropped, and the turn's `outcome`, `notebook`
and `journal` survive. That is the right trade and it is not in question.

WHAT IT COST. Before, a malformed `bugs` field failed loudly and took the proof
with it. Now it vanishes and NOTHING ANYWHERE RECORDS THAT IT EXISTED. A worker
that hit real friction, wrote it up, and shaped the JSON wrong has its report
silently discarded; the attempt record shows a clean `proved` with no bugs
filed, which is indistinguishable from a worker that had nothing to report. The
board's population is now a lower bound with no error bar.

THE SHAPE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Three of us hit this independently on 2026-09-06
and only noticed it was one shape afterwards:

  - Fathom: a killed `gleam test` runner still prints a well-formed summary.
    "106 passed, 3 failures" while run_test had died as a module and 75 tests
    never ran against a true total of 181. See
    `a-green-suite-can-under-report-and-still-look-green`.
  - Rowan: filed a bug with a `python -c` whose backticks the shell ate,
    silently dropping a word from the body. It passed a byte-exact JSON
    round-trip and a schema check. Valid, well-formed, wrong.
  - Keel: this, introduced on purpose while fixing something else.

In each case the system produces a confident, well-formed report that is wrong,
and nothing downstream can tell. It is the same family as
`workers-are-addressable-and-it-is-not-recorded`, where an attempt's
events.jsonl is not merely incomplete but confidently complete and wrong, and as
`harness-caused-abandonment-is-scored-as-difficulty`. The board now has five
entries in this family and they are the most expensive thing on it, because
every other entry assumes the records mean what they say.

CANDIDATE FIX, not chosen, and deliberately not built in the same change that
created the gap. Cheapest and probably right: `Report` gains a field naming what
was discarded, and the dispatcher logs it into the attempt's events.jsonl. It
prevents nothing and repairs nothing — it restores attributability, which is
what this whole family actually needs, and it is the same shape as the guard
logging its denials. Anything stronger (rejecting the turn, asking the worker to
resend) reintroduces the failure this fix just removed.

DO NOT resolve this one by making the decoder strict again. That is the bug that
was just closed.

bugs.title: CLAUDE.md forbids switching the shared checkout but never says what it sits on
bugs.body:
Raised by Rowan on 2026-09-06 and left to Keel because closing it means editing
CLAUDE.md, which needs Dib.

WHAT HAPPENED. The shared checkout C:/Users/dibuj/dev/rule30 sat on the feature
branch keel/bug-board all evening, ending up 20 commits behind main. Rowan
fast-forwarded it to main at Dib's direction after verifying the branch was a
strict ancestor. Nothing was lost. The question is why it was possible.

THE GAP, EXACTLY. CLAUDE.md says "The shared checkout has live sessions in it.
Never `git checkout` a different branch there" — a rule about what you must not
DO to that tree. It never says what the tree should be PARKED ON. So a checkout
that drifts onto a feature branch and stays there violates nothing, and the rule
forbidding a checkout is then the very thing that keeps it stuck: nobody may
move it back either.

DIB'S PREFERENCE, stated 2026-09-06: the shared checkout is always on main, and
branch work happens in worktrees.

WHY IT IS MORE THAN TIDINESS. The tree's branch is the default base for anything
started in it, and CLAUDE.md's own worktree section says both of this project's
worktree failures were staleness rather than collision. A shared tree parked on a
feature branch is the same failure with a wider blast radius, because every
session that starts there inherits it silently. It nearly bit twice tonight:
Rowan almost committed a main-destined registry row onto keel/bug-board, and
Fathom flagged that anything running `gleam test` in that tree was testing
harness code without the ports fix or seed.gleam.

FIX: one sentence in CLAUDE.md's "Changing the framework" section saying the
shared checkout is parked on main, alongside the existing rule about not
switching it. NEEDS DIB -- CLAUDE.md is his.

WORTH SAYING PLAINLY: this is a rule that was followed and still produced the
bad state, which is the useful kind of finding. The rule was about the action,
and the hazard was the resting state.

bugs.title: Two test runners write and delete the same fixture file
bugs.body:
Measured by Fathom on 2026-09-06 against a Keel suite running concurrently.
Filed by Keel, who holds blueprint/bugs.json; Fathom supplied the measurement
and asked for it to be its own entry rather than a paragraph on
`offline-fixtures-write-into-the-live-checkout`. That is the right call and the
reason is the useful part: THAT BUG'S PREMISE IS ONE RUNNER KILLED MID-TEST.
THIS ONE HAPPENS TO TWO RUNNERS THAT ARE BOTH PERFECTLY HEALTHY. Different
premise, different fix, different closure test, so folding them would have made
one entry that is half-fixed forever.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. Fathom's run: `193 passed, 4 failures`, all four at
verify_test.gleam:97 -- `let assert Ok(False) = simplifile.is_file(path)`, the
guard that refuses to start when the fixture file already exists. Going to look
at the leftover found it GONE and the shared checkout clean. A leftover that is
not there afterwards is not a leftover. Keel had reported `195 passed` five
times from another worktree over the same window; both suites were writing and
deleting one file.

THE CAUSE. `probe_id` was a `const`, and `dag.proof_path` derives the file name
from the id, so every runner on this machine resolved the same absolute path.
`HARNESS_REPO_ROOT` does not separate them: both worktrees default it to the
live checkout, because that is the only checkout with a built `.lake`.

CORRECTED 2026-09-06, before anyone acted on it. The entry as first filed said
the destructive direction was "not observed, reachable by inspection". THAT WAS
WRONG, AND KEEL WROTE IT WITHOUT WALKING THE GUARD IT DEPENDS ON. Fathom
analysed the interleavings from the code and Keel confirmed the ordering:
verify_test.gleam:132 checks `is_file` BEFORE the write at :133 and the delete
at :136, and a failed `let assert` panics the test, so a runner that finds a
peer's file aborts and never reaches the delete. Four aborts, zero deletes --
which is exactly what was measured.

So the guard works better than its own docstring claimed: for a killed runner it
turns loss into litter, and for a CONCURRENT runner it turns the destructive
path into a loud abort.

WHAT REMAINS. A narrower window where both runners pass the `is_file` check
before either writes. Both then write, both verify, both delete, and the second
delete fails its own assertion. Every interleaving ends loudly and in
verify_test:

  - `accepts_a_real_proof_test` reading the `sorry` body gets `ContainsSorry`
    and fails `is_verified`.
  - `rejects_sorry_test` reading a valid body gets a verdict that is not
    `ContainsSorry` and fails its `let assert`.
  - `rejects_wrong_statement_test` reading anything else fails its
    `let assert CheckFailed`.
  - A peer's delete landing before `lake build` reads the file gives
    `CheckFailed`, failing whichever test expected otherwise.

NO INTERLEAVING PRODUCES A WRONG VERDICT THAT PASSES. Analysed from the code by
Fathom, not observed, and that is weaker evidence than the collision itself,
which was measured.

WHY THE CORRECTION MATTERS MORE THAN THE ERROR. This board's expensive entries
are the silent ones, and filing a loud bug under a silent-corruption heading
dilutes the category that is doing the work. The severity stays `friction` for
the same reason: it costs a suite run and half an hour chasing a phantom, and
that is what it costs.

THREE READINGS OF ONE FILE AND ONLY THE THIRD IS RIGHT. Rowan saw the file
appear and read it as litter from a killed runner. Keel ruled
`offline-fixtures-write-into-the-live-checkout` stays open on the strength of
the same reading. Fathom looked for the leftover, found it absent, and got the
